Professor Boyd Dawkins, in his recent inaugural address as Presider.t of the Manchester Geological Society, called attention to certain geologies! points in reference to the water supply of Lancashire and Cheshire His general conclusions were—first, that in the area of Lanchire and Cheshire there was a v Ist lake, fed by subterranean water ; secondly, that the most advantageous mode of getting at it was by sink- ing deep welts; and, lastly, that the vacuum caused !y pumping at great depths would be more rapidly sup- plied by percolation from the surface of rain anct river water than near to the surface.

div.p: THE IRON TRADE AND FOREIGN TARIFFS.

A. memorandum drawn up by the British Iron Trade Association has been forwarded to the Foreign Oft' e through the Associated Chambers of Commerce. The Memorandum refers to the fact that in March, 1876, a communication was received from the President of the Associated Chambers of Commerce, enclosing a letter addressed to that body by the Earl of Derby, as Foreign Minister, expressing a desire to be informed as to the state of the British iron trade at that time. Inquiri.li were made by the, Association, and a report, summarised in the memorandum, was drawn up. The effect of the report was that the iron trade of Great Britain was in a state of unprecedented depression, and that the depression was not confined to Great Britain, but was felt on the Continent with nearly equal severity, and also in the United States. The memorandum con- cludes as follows "England possesses a marvellous capacity for producing iron and steel at, low rates, and could, undoubtedly, command the markets of the world, were they not, to a great extent, closed against her by hostile tariff... She adaiits, practically, with absolute freedom, the produce of nearly every other country, and it seems but reasonable that in return for the advantages which, herself receiving, England thus confers upon other countries, she should enjoy an equally free outlet for her own produce, and e4pecially for iron, her great natural staple, and an a. tiele which plays a leading part in the economy of nations."

The CHAIRMAN stated that there had been a meeting of the Ladies' Committee, and he felt bound to say that the boarding out of pauper children was not satis- factory and was most expeinuve, am' the idea that be- cause children were boarded out they would hear nothing of the workhouse was a fallacy. The children were threatened by the people with whom they lived that they would be sent back to the Workhouse, and in that -way they would hear more about the Work- house than they would if visited once a month or six weeks by the relieving officers. One of the boarded- out ohilcen had been absent 16 times from school in one quarter, one had been working in the fields although she was kept by the guardians. Had a relieving officer visited the case he would have reported it. • Mr. PAIR stated that he had heard of one case in the Aston district, where it had been stated that the schoolmaster had tied the child's petticoats and hoisted her to the top of the school by them. (Shame.) The child denied it he understood through shame, but some of the little girls in the school stated that it was true, and that the Odd played truant five days in conse- quence. However some of the children who were boarded out were most comfortable and well taken care of, and were doing remarkably well. He did not agree with the Chairman, that the children heard of the Workhouse, and he was satisfied that they would grow up unaware of the existence of the Workhouse, and he hoped that by means of boarding out, the ap- parently hereditary principle of pauperism would be stamped out. If they allowed the relieving officers to interfere with the boarded out children, the interest of the ladies committee in the children would be greatly affected. There might be a sine° case which was not satisfactory, but he strongly protested lagaiust any interference by the relieving officers whatever. (Laughter.) Mr. Kiammi, in the course of some remarks on the Bubj eat, said that the ladies were not there to stand up for their rights, and this was a time of day when they were not very baehful in doing that. (Laughter.) Mr. ATTICINS observed that it would be better to have lady Guardians. They had a woman as Over- seer in his township, and she acted moat famously. (Laughter.) After some discussion, in which a motion and an amendment were proposed and withdrawn, the subject dropped, the Board deciding to consult the Lattice' Committee before taking any action.

ALLEGED INGENIOUS THEFT AT ALTRINOHAM.

Francis Morley of Peel-street, Hale-road, Altrinc- ham, who has for some years resided in Altrincham, and has carried on the. business of repairer of china, was charged at the Altrincham police court, on Friday before Mr. Carlisle, with stealing a parse containing 9s. id., the money and property of Miss Storer, of Bowdon, on the 22nd inst., under the following some- what extraordinary circumstances. Miss Storer who resides in Prussia-terrace, Bowdon, stated that on the day in question, at about a quarter past three in the afternoon, she went to Altriucham. She had then a red leather purse with a brass clasp to it in her pocket. The purse contained lie. Id. in money. She paid 2s. in Altrincham. She called at Xlr. Royle's shop, and after leaving, and when near Miss Wiliiamson's school, in Ashley-road, she missed her purse. Her purse was safe when she left Royle's shop, and she had only got a distance of about 100 yards when she missed it. She turned back immedia- tely, and saw Mrs. Wood, and from what she told her she ascertained that a little boy had picked her purse up. John Rutter, a boy who found the purse, stated that he folio wed some ladies to try and find the owner. The prisoner came after him and said "Here, that is my purse." Witness had the purse in his pocket. He took the purse out of his pocket, and prisoner took it out of his hand. Prisoner.—Didn't I say to you when you picked the purse up, "It belongs to a lady who has gone into Smith's shop P" Witness.—No.

Prisoner.—Didn't I say it must belong to one of the ladies who has gone across the road? Witness.—When you came up to me you said, "Here, that is my purse," and you did not say it be- longed to a lady across the way. I saw the prisoner go up to a lady who came out of Smith's shop, after he had taken the purse from me, but I did not hear him speak to her, A boy named Ackerley, Thomas Morgan, and Mrs. Wood gave corroborative evidence. Thomas Morgan in reply to the prisoner said that prisoner did say "Go to that lady and see if it is her purse." AotingiSergeant Hervey stated that he apprehended the prisoner, who in reply to the charge said "You are wrong." On the way to the police-station he said that he was not in Altrinoham at all on Wednes-

day. Prisoner, who had no witnesses to call, said that he met the boys and saw them pick the purse up. He shouted to them to go to a lady who was coming out of Smith's shop, as he thought, and ask her was it her purse. The boys did, and she said it was not hers. He called the boys to him, and told Rutter to put the purse in his pocket, and to go to two ladies who were crossing the road and ask if they had lost anything. The boys ran after the ladies, as he thought, and something drew his attention across the way, and as he noticed the boys rosining in a different direction from the ladies he ran after the boys, and said, "The owner of the purse is in one of those two shops, Cooke's or Smith's, and when tte got to Cooke's the lady whom he thought owned the purse was coming out, and he asked her if else had lost anything. She said she had not. He went on to Smith's shop and asked a lady there if she had lost anything, and she said she had not, so he put the purse in his pocket, picked uit his basket, and walked demi Oxford-street with his wife. He opened the purse and examined it, and it contained two hall-crows, three shillings and a sixpence. He thought he would take it home with him and see if it was advertised. Ho had no intention of stealing the purse or its contents, and he was .( moithered " when the policeman came to him. On being 4harged with the theft he did not know what answer to make him. The purse was still in his cupboard. The prisoner was committed to take his trial at the Hutt term] Quarter Sessions.

div.head: RENT OF LAND. LECTURE AT BOWDON.
div.p: RENT OF LAND. LECTURE AT BOWDON.

The seventh of a series of lectures on political economy was delivered in the Parisis Church School° room, Bowdon, on Friday evening, by the Rev. W, Cunningham. The lecturer said that he had to dis- course that evening, not with the production of wealth, but with its distribution. With regard to the condi- tions under which land was held by the occupier, he would Bay many circumstancee tended to modify the rental. The competition for land was much governed by customs and relics of the feudal system still actively surviving, for instance there was the political consideration, A landlord preferred very often to have a tenant of the same political opinions as himself, who would vote with him; and as far as this was the case he did not let the land from purely economical considerations, and this relationship between landlord aud tenant came in to modify and prevent him getting such a large rent as he would otherwise do. One did not look upon these customs as being either very good or very bad; but what he wanted to point out was that things were not entirely determined by competition. Labour, capital, and land were the three things that played the part in this production of wealth, they were the three things which were rewarded in the distribu- tion of wealth, and throughout, competition was the force which distributed and allotted how much each should get. With respect to the great,disparhy iu the prevailing rate of wages, it was difficult to form a judgment, and it was scarcely less easy to understand toe causes that regulated toe rent of land. He had previously spoken about the reduced and reducing re- turns from land. Ile would suppose they took two farms, one a very good one, and the other a bad one. There would be a great difference in the ainouut of proauee that was got from these farms. He wanted than ilis'. to think of the gross amount of return, not of the rate of return which the farmer got on his capital. lid would take a very simple case, and imagine two farms which were exactly the same size, which had got the same number of labourers at work upon them, which were farmed in exactly the same way, that was to say, with the same sort of machinery so far as it was applie able in each case—at any rate, 1 that they had the same amount of capital and the same amount of labour; but the one farm was much better than the other, BO nineh Bo that a thousand more bushels of wheat were got . Irons the one farm than were got from the ' other. They were the same in every possible way, in the labour and the capital that was expended on them; but the one was very much better than the other in the quality of the sort. Now, who got those thousand bushels The labourers could not get it. The labourers on the better farm could not get any higher wages than the labourers on the worse farm, and that the labourers on the worse farm would be paid just as much aelhklabourers on the better farm, because they supposed that competition was at work, and that this came in to equalise their wages. Neither could it be got by the farmer, because at the end of the year, or when the lease was out, other farmers would come in, and the competition of farmers with farmers would prevent any one of them making such an immense deal more profit than the rest, so that if it did not go to the labourers, and did not go to the farmers, it • must go to the man who owned the land. The lecturer proceeded to illustrate the subject with a great and lucid cogency, and made it perfectly clear to the audience that he had mastered in an unusual manner some of the most abstruse problems in the science of political economy. --

RE-OPENING OF ST. MARY'S CHURCH.

The ceremony .of re-opening. Bt. Mary's Catholic Church, Widnes, after having undergone certain com- prehensive alterations, which embrace the addition of a handsome chancel from plans prepared by Mr. Ppgin, was observed on Sunday. There was high mass in the morning, and at this the e Most Rev. Dr. O'Reilly, Roman Catholic Bishop of the diocese, made his first official visit to theAeighbourhood, and preached an eloquent sermon to a large and attentive congrega- tion. His lordship explainea that in visiting Widnes he was carrying out a duty which was incumbent upon him, in order that he might remit to the Holy Bee a complete statement of the religions condition of the diocese of which he had charge, and for the reason that the Holy Father the Pope, who had the care of all the churches, required an exact return of religion throughout the whole of the Christim world. It was necess try for the Pope to be informed as to the re- quirements of his children, and of the extent to which they availed themselves of their religious privileges, and that being so, he would ask what kind of a state- ment he should be compelled to return as truthfully representing the condition of the Catholics of Widnes. The church, which had just been enlarged, was not yet what it should, and no aoubt soon would, be; and not only so, for the time was not very long distant when they would have to oensider the necesuty of providing another house of prayer, and when he would have to secure for them the services of additional priests. Dr. O'Reilly then referred to the shortcomings of Catho- lics in the neigabourhood, and urged upon his con- gregation increased attention to the ordinance of the Church in the future. There were in Widnes 7,000 Catholics, and 1,400 were returned as hearing mass, although that number could scarcely be regarded as representing regular attendants. He should also have to report to the Holy Father that only one in six went to the confessional. But the picture did. not end here, for the parents were not only neglectful of their own salvation, but they were careless as to the future well-being of their children. There were from 1,100 to 2,200 Catholic children between the ages of five and thirteen,who shooed attend day school, aud yet there were but 900 on the school rolls, showing not only irregular attendance, but a large number who were never sent to school at all. This sad condition of things was attributable to the sin of sloth, drunkenness and tbe.gratitication of the passions. The preacher spoke against early courtships and marriages between the different religious sects and distrait members of the same family. In the evening the preacher was the Rev. Father Nugent.

On Monday afternoon; Mr. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at Runcorn, on the body of Joseph Evans, the mate of St. Winifred, steam tug, belonging to the Bridgewater Navigation Co., the deoeased having died under most peculiar circumstances. The deceased, who was a man of intemperate habits, but who was formerly a teetotaller and a Sunday school teacher for seven years, went on board his vessel at Runcorn at half-past two on Tuesday afternoon, and he was then the worse for drink. Soon after, the boat was on its way t Liverpool, and the deceased was found in the middle cabin partially comatose, and the captain and crew thinking he was drunk left him lying in the cabin, one of the hands occasionally refreshing him with drinks of warm tea. Four voyages, to and from Liverpool, were made, the deceased, meanwhile, lying in what appeared to them to be a drunken stupor. On making the fourth voyage to Runcorn he was hoisted out of the cabin, taken on shore, and put in an empty hut without fire, and left there until discovered by his wife, who had him taken home on a stretcher, where he died three hours after.

Edward Davies, the superintendent of steam tugs at Liverpool, said it was a captain's duty to report a case of drunkenness to the harbour master in the ab- sence of the superintendent, and the offender would have been at once suspended. If the man was in a helpless condition the harbour master would take steps to gat him removed. Evans had been a master, and had been dismissed for drunkenness, and was only taken ou again on signing the pledge ; a pledge card was produced from the Liverpool Young Men's Christian Association, dated April let, 1876, and signed "Samuel Nash," with the words "Be thou fiithful unto death."

'jhe Coioner : Excuse me, gentlemen, 1 must have order during the inquiry. The examination of the witness was resumed, and Davies said that it was the captain's duty to have put the deceased on shore at Liverpool on making his first voyage. Thomas Rawlimion, harbour master of Duke's Dock, Liverpool, said Leech, the captain, reported that the deceased was drunk, and he gave him another man in his Dime, but did not order him to be removed, as there was no place to take him to at one o'clock in the, morning. Mr. Collier again proceeded with his cross-examina- tion, when he was again called to order, whereupon he replied to the Coroner—" Ah, you wouldn't like to hear one of my. orations for an hour, would you ?" (Laughter.) The Coroner t I should not. (Renewed laughter.). Dr. McDougall said he saw the deceased before death, and iound him complaining of much pain. He said he had fallen dow is the hold in the steamer. Upon making a post-mortem examination of the body he found that death had resulted from congestion of the lungs, supervening upon coldness and exposure, and want of proper medical treatment. He believed that the titan had fallen down the hold and rcoeived concus- sion of the brain. A. man could Rot continue in a state of drunkenness for 21 hours unless exposed to great cold. Had the man been landed on Wednesday morn- ing there would have been a chance of saving his life. The Coroner, in summing up, said there was no dis- pute as to the cause of death after the doctor's evi- dence, but it was just a question whether the captain had acted as a man possessing common sense, , and according to the dictates of common humanity. The jury were then looked up in an adjoining room, and after a sharp discussion they returned the fol- lowing verdict—' That Joseph Evans died from con- gestion of the lungs, supervening upon cold, exposure, and want of proper medical care; the jury wish to express their regret that he was not removed from the steamer earlier, but think that no blame is attributable to any particular person." " THACKERARY'S IRISH CHARACTERS."

On Monday evening the third lecture of the present Ea ries of "Lectures for the People " was delivered in the Public Hall, Warrington, by Mr. Hadfield (the Editor of this paper), who had chosen for his subj ect " Thackeray's Irish Characters." In the absence of Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., the Rev. H. W. Perris occupied the chair, and after apologising for the absence of Mr. Crosfield, introduced the lecturer to the meeting.

Mr. HADFIELD, who was greeted with applause' said: When my friend Mr. Perris invited me to en- deavour to de something pleasantly to oecupy one of these evenings at the Public Hall, it was impossible to refuse him because he said it could be done so easily. My professional experience, however, ought to have reminded me of a saying that " easy reading is exceed- ingly hard writing," and when the writing only con- sists of a few desultory and introductory observations it still demands time, and thought, and no inconsider- able amount of labour, Mr. Perris happened to knows however, that I had not merely read Thackeray's books, but had been greatly charmed with that great author's sketches .of Irish character, and he imagined that he had. furnished me with a" Reading made Easy." Sometime since I had jotted down in a dis- cursive sort of way, one or two ideas on the subject of these characters, and had hopedk.that one day these rough preliminary notes might develope themselves into a more philosophic shape and assume a more serviceable literary order. But man—and newspaper man especially—proposes, and "circumstance, the un- spiritual god," as Byron has it, remains master of the situation. What lam able to present to you on this fertile subject I present with all its imperfections on its head, and hope that it may obtain your general in- dulgence. In thinking over some of Thackeray'd studies of lush character the question may suggest it- self. How fer is the reader required to regard them as eccentric individual sketches, or as faithful crea- tions of the national portraiture? On reflection, I cannot suppose that Thackeray ever seriously meant to furnish materiala for a generalisation evi,ently based on caricature. No one, I think, can reasonably imagine that in the characters of Captain MatsSlaane ; in Major or Peggy O'Dowd ; in Captain Oostigan or the Fotheriegay ; or yet in Captain Shandon or his lieutenant and sub-editor Jack Irtuucane, that Thackeray ever designed to do more than is done by any literary artist of high creative capacity, to set before us in bold relief a few peculiar features of character, easily recognisable and necessarily marked —for artistic purpuies— with a distinct and apm eci- able amount of exaggeration. I take it, tberefore, that Mr. Thackerys Costiglias and O'Llowde were meant to be individual and not national portraits, freely and broadly treated by their artist maker. For all this. lam somewhat apprehensive that, owing to the singular force of Thackeray'a genius aid the vivid and startling way in which he has been able to breathe the breath of life into his own creations, that they are powerfully liable to be accepted by the Eng- lish people as authentic representations of the Irish nation. As, in my opinion,. this would be a mischiev- ous mistake and a grave juju/nice, I cannot help feel- ing that we are bound to make certain ample reserva- tions in favour of Ireland and the Irish character whenever we enter the famous and wonderful portrait gallery which Thackeray has created. If we wish to be just, it seems to me indispensable to remember that whether it be literary, dramatic, or pictorial art, the power of art to convey and establish erroneous impres- sions of national character is so great that it is.scarcely calculable. That power is almost absolute when such inaccurate impressions relate to individuals or a people with whom we have only limited opportunities of in- tercourse or can only observe under exoeptional and artificial circumstances. How few of us have seen the Irishman at home Besides London newspaper correspondents and commercial travellers, and the handful of tourists who in the summer and autumn rush to the Lakes of Killarney, or take a hurried peep at the Wicklow Mountains, there are 'not many of us who ever enter Ireland. Under these circumstances, I suppose it is natural that we should mistake the most broadly humorous sketches as examples of faithful portraiture. We know that the Irishman of the Eog- fish stage a hundred years ago long held his place in England as the typical Irishman. lint in later years we have become aware that the Irishman of eur last century farces—aad indeed of a considerable part of the preseut century—were really the most outrageous caricatures. In the same way the Frenchman of the British drama has long since been discovered to be an impossible creature; and the Englishman of to- day—l mean, of course, the Englishman of the com- fortable classes, who can afford to travel, who runs over to Paris, perhaps of toner than he runs down to Birmingham—has long since found out that the Gaul of the Empire or the Republic—or whatever else for the moment—happens to dominate the boulevards, is a wonderfully dissimilar creature to the typical Frenchman presented on the stage or the circulating library of our respected but undiscriminating grand- fathers. The greatness of the power exercised by the literary act—and exercised, too, in this particular re- lation—was illustrated, I to ink, in a very striking way by Thackeray himself in or about the year 1848 what we may call the year of Revolution. Some of us may remember that about that time the Young Ire- land party, led by the late John Mitchell and others, exerted an extraordinary authority over the young and impulsive spirits who at that time had been taught to dream the dream of Irish independence. The movement,-as we elders very well remember, was very suddenly and almost utterly extinguished. It is true that the Government of the time, adopted severe measures of repression, and that John Mitchell and several of his daring colleagues in rebellion were transported. It was the prevailing opinion, however, at that time that the extinction of the Young Ireland party was due, not BO much to the repressive measures of the Government as to that masterly and immoral satire written at that time by Mr. Thackeray for the pages of lima, and known to everybody as "The Battle of Limerick." I believe that from the day of its publication the Young Ireland ,party—as a party of any political significance—began to disappear, and in a very short time it was as completely extin- guished as was the chivalry of Spain, which was said to have died under the smile of Cervantes. I trouble you with these desultory observations not with the idea of criticising one of the Collossi of English litera- ture, nor yet with the intention of suggesting that Mr. Thackeray' in his studies of Irish character was ever consciously desirous of doing it injustice. But the charm of the great master's art is irresistible, and he had the giant's strength, which is perhaps never wholly unaccompanied by the giant's temptation. The first time Mr. Thackeray ever attempted any por- traiture of Irish character, so far as I can discovet, oc- curs in the novel of " Catherine," a work which ap- peared in 1839-40, and was published in " Fraser s Magazine." In a publisher's note appended to one of the latest editions of "Catherine," the book is described as written by Mr. Thackeray." to counteract the in- jurious influeme of some popular fictions of that day, which made heroes of high way mea and burglars, and created a false sympatny for the vicious and the crindual." The lrishmau who figures in this story of " Catherine " is one Captain IdacShaue. Tao story is labrin the time of Queen Anne ; but time will not permit us to describe or follow the plot, which is the less necessary seeing that our dealings with it-are con- fined to a single character in the story—Thackeray's first Irish sketch—Captain Mac Shane. The general tendency and complexion of the book may be pretty well inferred from the note I hsve quoted, and the reader of " Catherine " is introduced to perhaps the prettiest company of rascals that can be imagined to have existed in this kingdom in the year of grace 1705. Poor Captain. Macbhane appears to have easily fallen into this evil society, and to have carried into the busi- ness of the highwayman a personal daing and the oddest notions of military honour and chivalry. My reading front this book is little long, but the scenes are consecutive, and convey a tolerably complete pic- ture of the hero—the Captain. I may say that this gentleman was leaned indifferently, Ensign, Mr., or even Captain 111acShaue. His intimates occasionally, in sport, called him " Nosey," from the prominence of that feature in his Countenance. The Captain, as I have indicated, becomes one of the band of highway- men, who rob under the pretence of recruiting for the King's army. Mac Shane mission is to extort ransom for a captive, whom they persist in regarding as are omit, from the prisoner's parents. ; The Cuuntatan said he was sure the thanks of the meeting were due to Mr. Hadfield, who had afforded them so much amusement and instruction. It was sometimes a risk to exhibit to a miscellaneous audience pictures of irregular conduct, but he was satisfied that no formal lecture on " Intemperatice " could have rendered greater moral service than the pictures from the pages of Thackeray presented to them by Mr. ' Hadfield that evening.
A vote of thanks to the lecturer and chairman oloeed the proceedings./

Sir,—Mr. Cross has made three speeches at Birming- ham, and has taken credit in a remarkable manner for many measures that have been passed by the Liberal party. He attempts to appropriate the watchwords of the Liberals, "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform." I give his own words, "What minister in his senses would desire anything but peace!" (Cheers.) A pretty way of saying that Lord Beaconsfieid is not in favour of war with Russia! Or is Mr. Cross sarcastic, and does be mean that Lord Beaconsfield was not in his senses when he made that foolish and reckless speech at Guildhall—a speech calculated to fan the flames of war, and specially intended to fling defiance in the face of the Emperor of Russia. Was Mr. Cross aware of the despatch sent by Lord Loftus (Nov. 2nd) in which the Emperor of Russia solemnly declares that he never had any intention to take Constanti- nople p This despatch was acknowledged by Lord Derby, and must have been known to the Prime Minister when he spoke on the 9th November p The danger of this country being led into war is solely due to the fact that we have a Tory Ministry in power. Mr. Cross may say what he chooses, and may reiter- ate the question " What mall in his senses would de- sire war F" I tell him that there always has been far more da -ger of this country being led into war by a Tory than by a Liberal aimmistration. Mr. Cross says "In this great Eastern Question from beginning to end Her Majesty's Government have had but one desire, which was to maintain the peace of Europe !" ' Then what has Mr. Cross to say about be speech at Guildhall, on the 9th P More wicked and warlike words could not be cho en ; their spirit is palpably op- posed and inimical to peace. Mr. Cross must not sup- pose that the peapie of England are so besotted as not to detect the terrible humbug of dubbing Lord Beacons- field a minister desiring peace. As regards retrenchment, Mr. Cross's defence of Tory extravagance is weakness itself. If he wished to give a fair comparison between Liberal and Tory ex- penditure, why did he not speak of the thxes taken off by Mr. Gladst me, and of the reduction of the National Debt by the Liberal Government It is dishonest in a man who tries to mislead the people. And how speciously puerile it is in Mr. Cross to cut down the 78 millions to the mere expense ot the civil Govern- ment, as if the national expenditure was not always considered in the lump sum! Let Mr. Cross explain hew it is that a Liberal Chancellor of the Exchequer ii always able to reduce taxation, whilst a Tory Chan- cellor almost invariably, if anything, increases it ? Now, a word about Mr, Cross's Reform. He says —" Now, the great social reforms which have been re- ferred to, and in whish I have been able to take a humble part, I believe are essential to the well-being of this community. No man can ,have spent any part of his life in our great towns, or have gone through them as I have, without seeing to what a depth of degradation many of our fellow-creatures are reduced, and what infinite pains, labour, and time must be taken before you can put them in such a position as to know what is right and what is wrong, what is life and what is death." This kind of seriousness is all very well, but what must the conscience of such a man as Mr. Cross be made of when (if he does not know it he ought to know it) he himself, personally and ministerially, is more guilty than any other living politician of having swelled and promoted the very misery and degradation he pretends to deplore. This is a dark and severe accusation, and I would not venture to make it, if it was not most indubitably true! Mr. Cross extended the hours for drinking from seven in the morning to six in the morning, and that single hoar in the day has tempted hundreds and thousands of poor men in all our large towns into drinking habits, and has incalculably in- creased and intensified the misery of their wives and children. There was no justification and no paliation for Mr. Cross' action in this " social reform !" The only semblance of a reason was that the Tory party got into power by means of the drinking interest, and therefore the Home Secretary to reward the publicans and brewers to extend their influence and enlarge their profits, passed an Act of Parliament which positively compels the opening of public-houses at eix o'clock in the morning. Mr. Cross seems at a loss to account for the down- fall of Mr. Gladstone's Government. it is no mystery to any reflective Englishman. I can tell him. It was not because that great minister reformed great evils (the Irish Church was one) ; it was not because he re- duced taxation and diminished the National Debt ; it WU not because he was in favour of -Peace, Retrench- ment, and Reform," but because Mr. Bruce, his Home Secretary, tried to stem the tide of the natianal drunkenness, and tried to pass an act which would curtail the hours for drinking. This roused the mighty power of the licensed victuAllers, and the Tories backed them up. Mr. Cross ought to be ashamed to speak of the shocking social condition of those miserable multi- Pules who are lost to the sense of:right and wrong, so long as he, by legislative means, has so largely helped his fellow creatures to their own deplorable degrada- tion. lam quite ready to give Mr. Cross credit for having made some effort to improve toe dwellings of the poor, but the good he wlli do in that direction is only as a drop of water in an ocean of misery directly due to that fatal hour in the morning, whin he so wickedly dedicated to the licensed victuallers of

England. I notice that Mr. Cross carefully avoided all mention of the drink traffic f He paid a good deal about "Freedom." Let any one real speech by the Archbishop of Yo,k, delivered in Mn. ohester last Tuesday, in which Dr. Thompson mentions " Freedom," and compare tits two speeches. A man has lost his Freedom when he is drunk, but it did not suit Mr. Cross to take that view of the matter. The two greatest curses in England, have been, and are, War and Drink, and as a rule, the Liberal party have always ranked themselves as enemies to these vast evils, whilst the Tory party have never failed to use them to serve their own base political ends, and to maintain an Infamous political advantage. div.head: LIBERAL LEGISLATION OF THE CENTURY; No. VI.—FIBST PART. IRELAND..
div.p: THE LIBERAL LEGISLATION OF THE CENTURY; No. VI.—FIBST PART. IRELAND..

Tux pacification of Ireland is still the states.. luau's crux. We have the strange con- tradictions of maiden assizes, and of an inability to get a conviction for the clearest cases of murder; of womanly chastity, an absence of minor crimes, and of the blackest and fou est treachery; of frank, generous, manly bearing, and of sneaking assassina- tion; of perpetual legislation for the coun- try, and of chronic discontent. Why is this? and what is the remedy? The Irish clamour for Home Rule while they have the evidence before them that an Irish parlia- ment was a complete failure, that each mem- ber had his price, and that with the purest and most patriotic representatives, self- government—in an imperial sense—could not be permitted by Great Britain, any more t an that the United States could permit subdivision of their Union. A historian says: "They have not yet acquired the elements of political education, and appear to be as far as ever from learning the first maxim of good government, the separation of political affairs from spiritual control." Till men learn to separate the civil from the ' ecclesiastical, and give each its due, good government is hopeless. Lord Russell, in treating of justice to Ireland, lays down six propositions with a view to a better govern- ment of that country, of which we give two or three, though we cannot agree with all of them.

I. "That murders in Ireland are not the insulated crimes of persons excited by covetousness or revenge, but the deliberate acts of a powerful confederacy, which, in defiance of the Queen and Parliament, orders the infliction of a criminal law more formidable than the law of the State." This proposition, he says, can be demon- strated both by authority and numerous instances. Lord Russell gives sufficient evidence to substantiate his proposition, but it is not now our province to follow it. IL "That the Roman Catholic clergy, in the capacity of Farish priests, have great sway over the minds of the people of Ireland ; but being entirely dependent upon the voluntary offerings of their flocks, are, from sympathy or from fear, unwilling to appear as the prosecutors of the confederacy that directs and executes murders."

That the priests have an enormous power over the people for good or evil is quite true, but we demur to the latter clause of the proposition. We do not think the priests yield to the people because of their salaries, any more than the dissenting ministers of Great Britain bemme the slaves of their congregations. It is far more probable that when the people are in earnest they will yield rather than lose their power. This we think was evidenced in the Fenian movement, which was at first opposed and then yielded to; just as in the early age of the Church the priests opposed old Pagan customs, but finding the people would adhere to them, the customs were adopted, and have become some of the most cherished rites of the Christian Church.

111. "That the remedy for these evils is to be sought in such a reform of the crimi- nal law as would place convictions for mur- der in the hands of the jury, and, secondly, in making a provision for the Roman Catholic parish priests of Ireland out of the revenues of the Protest nt Church, after the expiry of life interests, with a provisional grant in the interval from the Consolidated Fund." We cordially agree with the first clause of this proposition, but fail to see that the second would prove any more efficacious than the endowment of Maynooth has been. "That the Secretary of State for the Home Department of Cheat Britain ought to have in Ireland the same-powers of ad- ministration which he exercises in England and Scotland."

This is wise. Legislation should be in all respects as nearly equal as possible. There may be some local customs or privileges, long used and enjoyed, which may make this difficult, but broadly speaking, there should be no differences. But before we suggest remedies we must glance at past injustice, upon acts that we wish could be blotted out of the page of English history; acts which have left a mark upon the moral condition of the people, which will require many long years to efface. "Their virtues and fail. ings," says Mr. Massey, "were in an oppo- site direction to those which are found in people who flourish under free municipal institutions. Their failings were such as are bred by oppression and the denial of poli- tical rights: dissimulation and falsehood, reeklessnees, indolence, want of self-reliance. Their virtues were religious reverence, courage, fidelity. But their religion was a blind superstition; their courage, for want of proper training and a just direction, be. came wanton and mischievous; their fidelity, like that of another branch of the Celtic family, consisted in a passionate attachment to the old territorial aristocracy." The injustices which oppressed Ireland were manifold in their nature, and some of them of long duration. Ingenuity seems to have been taxed to the utmost to find a better system for crushing out the life of the people, or of driving them to the energy of despair. Can we expect the memory of these wrongs to pass away with a genera- tion P Our course is to be just and fear not. In commerce heavy exactions were levied. "The soil of Ireland," says Lord Russell, "is especially adapted to the feeding of sheep; the price of fleece-wool in Ireland, in 1733, was fivepence, of combed wool, twelve-pence a pound. In France, Irish fleece-wool was sold for two and sixpence a pound; combed wool from four shillings to six shillings. It is obvious that if the Irish had been allowed to export this fleece and combed wool to France, they would have made an enormous profit by their pastoral industry, and the anarchical spirit would have been vanquished. What stood in the way of these benefits—benefits for Ireland, benefits for England, benefits for the Em - pire ? Why could not the Irish build manufacturing towns, and erect manufac- tories of cloth in competition with the linen manufactories of Belfast, in rivalty of the towns of Leeds and Halifax in England? Was it the anarchical spirit of the Irish? No. When the Irish rebels with their French allies had been vanquished at the Boyne, when James had gone back to say his prayers and get absolution at S. Ger- maine, the English Parliament, instead of making a flourishing United Kingdom, pro- hibited, by Act of Parliament, the direction of the industry of the Irish to the manufac- ture of cloth, and in a spirit of detraction and of selfishness, resolved to build on the poverty of Ireland the suprem. acy of English law and English administration, When this monopoly had. gone on for century, and the Irish, deprived of faire ay l a o urse for their industry, had resorted
Amilisku escl migsolital Atoigh

o illegal trade, as the only defence against the injustice and impolicy of England, Mr. 'Hely Hutchinson, an Irish gentleman of noble family, made in 1779 the following statement before Lord Harcourt, the Lord Lieutenant :—"As the law stands,' he said, 'we can sell ot& wool and woollen goods only to Great Britain. We can buy woollen cloths there only. , If such a law related to two private men instead of two Kingdoms, and enjoined that in buying and selling the same goods, one individual should deal with one man only in exclusion of others, it Ivould in effect ordain that both as buyer and seller, that man should fix his own price and profit, t. id should refer to his discretion the loss and profit of the other dealer. You have defeated your own object. The exclu- sion of Ireland from the woollen trade has been more injurious to you than to us. One Ketof Irish wool works up two packs of ch wool. The French undersell the English, and as far as they are supplied with Irish wool, the loss to England is double what it would be, if the Irish ex- ported their wool manufactured. As to the practice of running wool, Ireland has paid to Great Britain for eleven years past, double the sum she collects from the whole world in all the trade which Great Britain allows her—a fact not to be paralleled in the history of mankind. Whence did all this money come? Our very existence is dependent on our illicit commerce."

div.head: DEATH OF SIR E. ARMITAGE.
div.p: DEATH OF SIR E. ARMITAGE.

Our readers will learn with sincere regret that Sir Elkanah Armitage died last Sunday at .his residence, Hope Hall, near Manchester. The venerable gentle- man who had attained the patriachal age of upwards of fourscore years, had been in his time, one of the most conspicuous figures in the county palettes, and he probably represented in his own personal character and history, the most remarkable and honourable traits that have bestowed on Lancashire an imperial place in the industry of the world. The d ficeased Knight had risen to well-earned opulence and social distinction from humble but honourable beginnings. He became what Mr. Bright once called" the prince of manufacture" in his Lime; also filled the highest municipal and other daces in the gift of hie fellow citizens of Manchester and Salford. Being Mayor of Mulches ter during the troublous Chartist times, when political oppression seemed to have broken down the prudence, as well as the patience, which ever governs successful political agitation the Mayor by his sympa- thetic and benign behaviour towards the malcontents averted considerable danger menaced by the inflam- mable materials which then seethed in the popular bosom. His sympathy with the sufferings of the peeple was unaffected, and his political principles were as much akin to their's, as they represented a broad and real scheme of popular liberty and popular repre- sentation. The deceased gentleman was one of the most eminent Liberal leaders in the North of England, although the place he chose in the Liberal ranks was ever modest and unassuming. He belonged to that historic race of English Nonconformists of whom it has been said that theirs was the "dissidence of Dissent," and his long life of more than four score years seems to cover an illustrious and memorable historic period, which has witneesed the very infancy of English liberty and Liberalism, until it rose to its very zenith, It will be well for England if the industry, the charity, the domestic virtues, the shining personal integrity, and the never-wearied public) spirit of the deceased patriarch should continue to constitute the beacons of Lancashire—of English character.

CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE. The annual meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture was held on Thursday, at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe. The Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P. presided. There was only a small attendance. The SECRETARY (Mr. T. Rigby) read the half-yearly report of the Council, which stated that since the general meeting in May they had taken no action beyond carrying out the arrangement with the trus- tees and head master of the SandbachGrammer School for the education of farmers' sons in the rwiiments of chemistry, botany, and animal physiology, in addition to the usual subjects taught at a public gram- mar sehool. It would be remembered that at the gene- ral meeting held at Rnntsford in October, 1875, it was resolved to accept the offet of the head master to take pupils as boarders, under the auspices of the chamber for £4O per year, and put them through the course of instruction named, provided 20 scholars were entered, or the sum of ten guineas was paid for any number less than 20. In the first quarter of the year 14 boys at- tended the school, 15 in the second quarter, 16 in the third, and the some number in the present quarter. The quarterly balances paid to the head master had amounted to £49 17s. ed. The council had, how- ever, received promises of subscriptions, to guarantee the chamber against any loss or charge upon its funds, amounting to £ll2 per year for ttree years. They had, therefore, now to call upon the guarantors for one half of the sums severally promised, which they had no doubt willingly subscribed; but the council most earnestly requested members to give their per- sonal influence in aid of the seheme, to as to render it self-sup orting in the future. There could be no doubt of the value of the education provided, nor that as time went on its value would be more appreciated. The times were changing, and success as a farmer would not in future be obtained so fully by simply holding or driving the plough as by the wise applica- tion of scientific knowledge. /t should be mentioned that the Lord-Lieutenant, the first president of the chamber, gave a scholarship of £2O per year tenable for two years to the most proficient scholar who had been born in Cheshire, and who was intended by his parents to be a farmer or land agent. The CHAIRMAN said that during the eight years the chamber had been in existence it had discuswad most of the public questions affecting agriculture both social, and political. At the present time there seemed to be a want of interest in their operations, which was not perhaps to be regretted, in so far as it showed that at the present time there was no grievance or burning question likely to come before Parliament. But if the chamber was to maintain its usefulness it must not confine itself to such subjects as those which had hitherto come before it, but must take action with re- I gard to the practical working of agriculture in the county. There were many questions which might be considered, such as the condition of the labourer, and the present style of farming as applied to a variety of the requirements of the day. They were told that It did not pay to grow wheat. They in Cheshire were not much affected by the low price of wheat ; but they were affected by the price of cheese, which was coming over from America, and by other things which influenced the markets all over the world. Then the question of the best system of dairy farming had- lately arisen, and there had been an interesting exhibition in London of the products of dairy farms. The consideration of sub. jecte such as these would perhaps bring together a large number of farmers, and really make the chamber a useful one in the country. Speaking of the questions which had come before Parliament in the last session, he said he had heard that some disappointment was felt that the Highways Bill, which had lobe postponed, did not give greeter relief to local taxation. The bill was not intended to give relief to local taxation, but to bring about a more economical administration of county roads and to concentrate their management. Another bill, which was earned by Sir Massey Lopes, relieved local taxation in connection with lunatic asy- lums. It had been proposed, and he hoped that a measure for the purpose would be introduced again next session, to further relieve local taxation by the transferring to the Government the cost of county prisons. That would give it in this county substantial relief. In Cheshire, prisons were well adminis- tered, but taking the country as a whole there was no doubt that they were not economically managed. The Education Act affected all industries. Its principle was that of indirect rather than direct compulsion. It was to be hoped that anything like direct compulsion mght be avoided by a feeling throughout the country —shared in both by farmers and farm labourers—that the education which was now offered should be taken advantage of. The act was one which should be worked with a great deal of care. In some of the large towns compulsion had been enforced; and it had been most successful where it had been enforced with great tenderness and leniency at first. As to the education of farmers' sons, he was glad that in 16 eases advantage had been taken of the arrangement between the chamber and the trustees of the Sandbach Grammar School, though he should have been better pleased if more boys had been sent there. He moved the adop- tion of tee report. Lord DE TABLEr seconded the motion, which wa passed. On the motion of LORD DE TABLET, seconded by Mr Parr, s. resolution was passed authorising application to the guarantors in connection with the Sandbach Grammar School scheme for half the amount which they had severally guaranteed. The president, the vice-presidents, the tree surer, and the secretary were re-elected. The retiring members of the council for East and West Cheshire were re-elected, with the exception of Mr. R. Bar- bour, in whose place Mr. Orion, of Tattenhall, was appointed, The Rev, G. Heron and Mr. Tomlinson were elected members for Mid-Cheshire, and Mr. Fair, was re- elected. This concluded the business of the meeting.

div.head: DEATH OF THE REV. DR. BEARD.
div.p: DEATH OF THE REV. DR. BEARD.

The Rev. Dr. Beard, a distinguished Unitarian Mi. ulster and the author of a great number of educational and other works published by Messrs. Cassel of Lon- don, died on Wednesday, at his residence, Ashton-on- Mersey. The venerable scholar was in the Mk year of his age. His ministerial career opened in 1825 with a poor and struggling Unitarian congregation in Sal- ford, which removed in 1843 to the spacious chapel in Strangeways, in the same borough. From this pas- torate, which he had held for 39 years, he removed to Altrinoham, shortly afterwards taking a ministerial charge at Sale, Cheshire. The late Dr. Beard, as we have said, was an able and voluminous author, his best known works being " Latin Made Easy," "Lessons in English," "Latin Dictionary," all published by Cas- sell; and Self Culture," published by Heywood. His theological writings are very numerous, and include " The People's Dictionary of the Bible," "The Auto. biography of Satan," " Christ the Interpreter of the Scriptures," &0., &e. He also engaged a good deal in translations from French and German, among whioh are " Reville's Life of Theodore Parker," Ravine's Manual of Religions Instruction," "Saint's History of Rationalism, "- Bousique's History of Christianity," " Schumann's Introduction to the Bible," and other works. He took great interest in all matters concern- ing the education of the people, and was one of the originators of the movement which resulted in the erection of the Albert Memorial Hall, Manchester, where the Unitarian Home Missionary Beard now car- ries on its business. All his life Dr. Beard laboured In the cause of the education of the people, he being one of a number of gentlemen, including the late Mr. Cobden, Mr. Alexander Ireland, Dr. Jona Watts, and others, who founded the Lancashire Public School As- sociation, an organisation which Afterwards assumed a national character, and which undoubtedly furnished materials for the legislation of recent years. He was the father of the Rev. Chao. Beard, of Liverpool.

div.head: AFFAIRS IN THE EAST
div.p: AFFAIRS IN THE EAST

Lord Salisbury, during the present week has been making an almost semi-royal pro- gress to the various capitals of Europe, where he has conferred with Prime Ministers and Emperors, and is doubtless accumula- ting material for the great Conference of the Powers, so soon to assemble. What will come of that Confer nee probably no human being can precisely foresee but it is to be hoped that as for all practical purposes it will be England and Russia that must furnish a solution of the present enormous European difficulty, some sane and dispassionate understanding may "oe shortly arrived at by these two Powers. The project of Constitutional reform with which Turkey has lately sought to amuse Europe, is not worth the paper on which it is written, and the Porte will hardly succeed again in imposing on the credulity of European Co. vernment. A political trick of this kind was tried twenty years ago, and it is idle to re- peat the experiment. The Times referring to the situation says: " Charity, a certain unsteadiness in intellectual resolution, or some other motive of weakness or of benevo- lence is ready to prompt them to give the Turkish government yet another oppor- tunity of showing that, if left to themselves, they can bring order out of chaos, justice out of misrule, and peace and freedom out of the anarchy of capricious oppression. The time for the plainest speaking on the Eastern Question is very near. The reti- cence of office imposes upon Ministers silence long after the time when patriotism compels the private citizen to speak, and it cannot be tolerated that there should be any longer any misapprehension at Constantinople of the policy of England." Lord Salisbury had an interview, on Wednesday, in Rome with Signor Melegari, the Italian Minister for Foreign Affairs. The reception which he met with in Berlin and Vienna has been observed, it is stated, with much interest at St. Patel sburg. His conversations with Prince Bismarck and Count Andrassy must have convinced him, it is considered, that the alliance of the three Empires remains intact, and that if the Czar has hitherto refrained from taking extreme measures, to which he has frequently been provoked, it has been out of consideration for the Emperors of Germany and Austria. At the Conference, Russia will maintain that an occupation of the Turkish provinces is the best means of guaranteeing their autonomy. If the other Powers refuse to join in this occupation, she will carry out tne measure single-handed.

The Russian Gaga, in a vehement article against the English Premier, alleges that he purposely kept back the reporL of the conversation which Lord A. Loftus had had with the Czar at Livadia, and, thereby con. coaled from the people of England the fact that Russia had engaged "to act disin. terestedly." From the general tenour of recent despatches it seems clear that the Moscissv speech was delivered "in a state of excitevient exceeding anything officially avowed in the course of the present reign." The 2imeB correspondent at Berlin asserts that the greater part of the Turkish armies are being pushed to the Danube. The North German Gazette, which pro- bably in this case speaks the mind of the Government, refers to Mr. Carlyle's sugges- tion that Prince Bismarck should be appointed arbiter of- the fate of Turkey. The Gazette accords a resp ctful hearicir to the suggestion, but politely rejects it, and then goes on to deride the attempt of Turkey "to anticipate the action of Europe by drawing the brightly coloured curtain of a seemingly constitutional comedy over the bloody drama of Bulgaria."
DIR. W. E. FORSTER, 1.1. P., ON THE EASTERN
QUESTION.

Mr. W. E. Forster, M.P., was presented On Monday with the freedom of the oity of Aberdeen. In acknow- ledging the honour, the right hon. gentleman delivered an address on the Eastern Question. He did not re- oollect any topic engrossing so much attention as this; and when a Prime Minister introduced into his speeches references to a possible campaign of 2 or 3 years' duration, it was not surprising that a keen in- terest should be felt in the matter. By such injudi- cious speeches Lord Beaconsfield had greatly increased the difficulties of the situation. Great Britain could never attain that cordial agreement with Russia, whioh was absolutely necessary to prevent a t•srribla war breaking out in Europe, so long as we bad an nn- founded suspicion of that country. Mr. Forster de- fended Russia's action and policy as perfectly fair ; and, alluding to the Conference, he hoped that Lord Salisbury would join with Russia in seeking to obtain guarantees and not mere promises from the Turkish Government, that they will no longer misgovern the Christian provinces in Turkey, and that at the same time they will relieve thesa provinces from the grossest oppression which almost any men have had to endure.

After referring to the losses sus- tained by the Crimean war, and contending that no good object was gained by the conflict, the address proceeds to say that the question seems about to be put before long to the British peoplo " Are you wil• ling to repeat the policy of 1858-4 Y" Will they con- sent, it is asked, that English bload and treasure shall be again poured forth to uphold the most execrable system of Government under the sun—a system doomed, as all incurably wicked and corrupt things are doomed, to perish from the face of the earth f, The address strongly urges the desirability of arbitration being re• sorted to in ease of disputes among nations.

div.head: REFORM UNION ON THE GOVERNMENT
div.p: THE REFORM UNION ON THE GOVERNMENT
WAR POLICY.

The Executive Committee of the National Reform Union have issued a memorandum to the branches with reference to the war policy of the Government. There is grave danger, they lay, that this country may at any moment be I lunged Into a dreadful and need- lesskwar.:As a consequence of Lord Beaoonsfleld's de. ularation, the signal for preparation, if not for actual conflict, has been sounded in Europe. Russia and Austria are arming, and in our own country active military preparations are on foot. The committee urge the branches to use every exertion to rouse public feeling against the war policy of the Government, and say The country has been told that it is an un- patriotic thing to embarrass the Government by agitations during a time of delicate and difficult negotiations. We reply that we feel it our duty to prevent the Government embarrassing the country by a war which we could under no circumstances ap- prove, and against which we new solemnly and em- phatically protest."

THE "PALL MALL GAZETTE" AND THE "TIRES." It is not often that the Times condescends to reply to a leader in another newspaper. It has done so this week. On one page it quotes an extraordinary artice in the Pall Mall Gazette, and in its leader page that aTticle is answered. The answer is very cogent. It is to the effect that the Pall Mall admits that Ger- many wishes to see Russia destroyed, but that, as she cannot undertake the matter for herself, England ought to do it for her. Why England should do it there is no attempt to show. The Times urges, on the other hand, more strongly than ever, that England should co-operate with Russia.
